paragraphs: 'Verified,' I say, not 'authorised'; for verification is only the testimony and the record, not the authority of the law, which consists in the command of the sovereign alone.

If, then, a man has a question of injury depending on the law of nature — that is, on common equity — the sentence of the judge who, by commission, has authority to take cognisance of such cases is a sufficient verification of the law of nature in that individual case. For though the advice of one who professes the study of the law is useful for avoiding contention, it is only advice; the judge must tell men what the law is, upon the hearing of the controversy.

But when the question is one of injury, or of crime, upon a written law, every man, by going to the registers (himself or through others), may, if he wishes, be sufficiently informed before he does the injury or commits the crime whether it is an injury or not. Indeed he ought to do so: for when a man doubts whether the act he is about to do is just or unjust, and may inform himself if he chooses, then to do it is unlawful. In the same way, the man who supposes himself injured in a case determined by the written law, which he himself or others may see and consider, acts unjustly if he complains before consulting the law, and betrays a disposition rather to vex other men than to demand his own right.

If the question is one of obedience to a public officer, to have seen his commission, with the public seal, and to have heard it read — or to have had the means to be informed of it, if a man wanted — is a sufficient verification of his authority. For every man is obliged to do his best endeavour to inform himself of all written laws that may concern his own future actions.

Once the legislator is known, and the laws — either by writing or by the light of nature — are sufficiently published, there is still another very important condition wanting before they are binding. For it is not the letter, but the intent, or meaning — that is, the authentic interpretation of the law (which is the sense of the legislator) — that is the nature of the law. And so the interpretation of all laws depends on the sovereign authority; and the interpreters can be none but those whom the sovereign (to whom alone the subject owes obedience) shall appoint. For otherwise, by the craft of an interpreter, the law may be made to bear a sense contrary to that of the sovereign — by which means the interpreter becomes the legislator.

All laws, written and unwritten, need interpretation. The unwritten law of nature, though easy to those who without partiality or passion make use of their natural reason — and therefore leaves its violators without excuse — has nevertheless, considering that there are very few, perhaps none, who in some cases are not blinded by self-love or some other passion, now become the most obscure of all laws, and consequently the one with the greatest need of able interpreters. The written laws, if short, are easily misinterpreted from the various meanings of a word or two; if long, they are more obscure still from the various meanings of many words. So that no written law, delivered in few or in many words, can be well understood without a perfect understanding of the final causes for which the law was made; the knowledge of which final causes is in the legislator. To him therefore there can be no knot in the law that is insoluble — either by finding out the ends that may untie it, or by making whatever ends he wills (as Alexander did with his sword in the Gordian knot), by his legislative power; which no other interpreter can do.
The authentic interpretation of the law is not the interpretation of writers.

The interpretation of the laws of nature, in a commonwealth, does not depend on the books of moral philosophy. The authority of writers, without the authority of the commonwealth, does not make their opinions law, however true they may be. What I have written in this treatise about the moral virtues, and their necessity for the procuring and maintaining of peace, though it is evident truth, is not therefore at once law; it is law because in all commonwealths of the world it is part of the civil law. For though it is naturally reasonable, it is by the sovereign power that it is law. Otherwise it would be a great error to call the laws of nature unwritten laws, of which we see so many volumes published — and in them so many contradictions, both of one another and of themselves.
The interpreter of the law is the judge, giving sentence viva voce in every particular case.

The interpretation of the law of nature is the sentence of the judge constituted by the sovereign authority to hear and decide such controversies as depend on it; and it consists in the application of the law to the present case. For in the act of judicature, the judge does no more than consider whether the demand of the party is consistent with natural reason and equity; and the sentence he gives is therefore the interpretation of the law of nature; which interpretation is authentic, not because it is his private sentence, but because he gives it by the authority of the sovereign — by which it becomes the sovereign's sentence, which is law for that time, to the parties pleading.
The sentence of a judge does not bind him, nor any other judge, to give the like sentence in like cases ever afterward.

But because no judge, subordinate or sovereign, is incapable of erring in a judgement of equity, if afterward, in another like case, he finds it more consistent with equity to give a contrary sentence, he is obliged to do it. No man's error becomes his own law, nor obliges him to persist in it. Nor (for the same reason) does it become a law to other judges, even if they have sworn to follow it. For though a wrong sentence given by authority of the sovereign — if he knows and allows it, in laws that are mutable — be a constitution of a new law, in cases in which every little circumstance is the same; yet in immutable laws, such as are the laws of nature, such sentences are no laws to the same or to other judges in like cases ever after. Princes succeed one another; one judge passes, another comes; nay, heaven and earth shall pass, but not one tittle of the law of nature shall pass, for it is the eternal law of God. So all the sentences of preceding judges that have ever been cannot together make a law contrary to natural equity; nor can any examples of former judges warrant an unreasonable sentence, or discharge the present judge from the trouble of studying what is equity (in the case he is to judge) from the principles of his own natural reason. For example, it is against the law of nature to punish the innocent; and innocent is the man who acquits himself judicially, and is acknowledged for innocent by the judge. Put the case now that a man is accused of a capital crime, and, seeing the power and malice of some enemy, and the frequent corruption and partiality of judges, runs away for fear of the outcome — and is afterwards taken, brought to a legal trial, makes it sufficiently appear that he was not guilty of the crime, and being acquitted of it, is nevertheless condemned to lose his goods. This is a plain condemnation of the innocent. I say therefore that there is no place in the world where this can be an interpretation of a law of nature, or be made law by the sentences of preceding judges who had done the same. For the one who judged it first judged unjustly; and no injustice can be a pattern of judgement for succeeding judges. A written law may forbid innocent men to flee, and they may be punished for fleeing. But that fleeing from fear of injury should be taken as presumption of guilt, after a man has already been judicially absolved of the crime, is contrary to the nature of a presumption — which has no place after judgement has been given. Yet this is set down by a great lawyer for the common law of England: 'If a man,' he says, 'that is innocent be accused of felony, and for fear flees for it; although he judicially acquits himself of the felony, yet if it be found that he fled for the felony, he shall, notwithstanding his innocency, forfeit all his goods, chattels, debts, and duties. For as to the forfeiture of them, the law will admit no proof against the presumption in law, grounded on his flight.' Here you see, an innocent man, judicially acquitted, notwithstanding his innocency (when no written law forbade him to flee), after his acquittal, on a presumption in law, condemned to lose all the goods he has. If the law grounds on his flight a presumption of the fact (which was capital), the sentence ought to have been capital; if the presumption were not of the fact, then for what should he lose his goods? This therefore is no law of England; nor is the condemnation grounded on a presumption of law, but on the presumption of the judges. It is also against law to say that no proof shall be admitted against a presumption of law. For all judges, sovereign and subordinate, if they refuse to hear proof, refuse to do justice; and though the sentence be just, the judges who condemn without hearing the proofs offered are unjust judges, and their presumption is mere prejudice, which no man ought to bring with him to the seat of justice, whatever precedent judgements or examples he may pretend to follow. There are other matters of this nature in which men's judgements have been perverted by trusting to precedents; but this is enough to show that, though the sentence of a judge is law to the party pleading, it is no law to any judge who succeeds him in office.

In the same way, when the question is the meaning of written laws, the man who is not the interpreter of them is the one who writes a commentary on them. For commentaries are commonly more open to cavil than the text, and so need other commentaries; and so there is no end of such interpretation. Therefore, unless there is an interpreter authorised by the sovereign, from whom the subordinate judges are not to depart, the interpreter can only be the ordinary judges, in the same way as they are in cases of the unwritten law; and their sentences are to be taken by the litigants as laws in that particular case, but not as binding other judges, in like cases, to give like judgements. For a judge may err in the interpretation even of written laws; but no error of a subordinate judge can change the law, which is the general sentence of the sovereign.

In written laws, men commonly distinguish between the letter and the meaning of the law. When by 'the letter' is meant whatever can be gathered from the bare words, the distinction is well taken. For the meanings of almost all words are either in themselves, or in their metaphorical use, ambiguous, and may be argued into many senses; but there is only one sense of the law. But if by 'the letter' is meant the literal sense, then the letter and the meaning, or intent, of the law are one and the same. For the literal sense is what the legislator is always supposed to intend by equity; and it would be a great affront for a judge to think otherwise of the sovereign. He ought therefore, if the words of the law do not fully authorise a reasonable sentence, to supply it with the law of nature; or if the case is difficult, to defer judgement until he has received more ample authority. For example: a written law ordains that the man thrust out of his house by force shall be restored by force. It happens that a man through negligence leaves his house empty, and on returning is kept out by force — for which case no special law has been made. It is plain that this case is contained in the same law; for otherwise there is no remedy for him at all, which must be supposed to be against the intention of the legislator. Again, the word of the law commands judging according to the evidence; a man is falsely accused of a fact which the judge saw himself done by another and not by the accused. In this case neither shall the letter of the law be followed to the condemnation of the innocent, nor shall the judge give sentence against the evidence of the witnesses — because the letter of the law is to the contrary; but he shall procure that another be made judge, and himself become witness. So the inconvenience that follows from the bare words of a written law may lead a judge to the intention of the law, and so to interpret it better — though no inconvenience can warrant a sentence against the law. For every judge of right and wrong is not a judge of what is convenient or inconvenient for the commonwealth.

The abilities required in a good interpreter of the law — that is, in a good judge — are not the same as those of an advocate; namely, the study of the laws. For a judge, as he ought to take notice of the fact from none but the witnesses, ought also to take notice of the law from nothing but the statutes and constitutions of the sovereign, alleged in the pleading or declared to him by some who have authority from the sovereign power to declare them; and he need not take care beforehand what he shall judge, because it shall be given him what he shall say about the fact, by the witnesses, and what he shall say on a point of law, from those who in their pleadings shall set it forth, and by authority interpret it on the spot. The lords of Parliament in England were judges, and the most difficult cases have been heard and determined by them; yet few of them were much versed in the study of the laws, and fewer had made profession of them; and though they consulted with lawyers appointed to be present there for that purpose, they alone had the authority to give sentence. In the same way, in the ordinary trials of right, twelve men of the common people are the judges, and give sentence, not only of the fact but of the right, pronouncing simply for the complainant or for the defendant — that is, they are judges not only of the fact but also of the right; and in a question of crime, they not only determine whether it was done or not done, but also whether it was murder, homicide, felony, assault, and the like, which are determinations of law. But because they are not presumed to know the law of themselves, there is someone with authority to inform them of it in the particular case they are to judge. Yet if they do not judge according to what he tells them, they are not on that account subject to any penalty, unless it can be shown that they did it against their consciences, or had been corrupted by reward. The things that make a good judge, or a good interpreter of the laws, are: first, a right understanding of that principal law of nature called equity — which, depending not on the reading of other men's writings but on the goodness of one's own natural reason and meditation, is presumed to be most in those who have had the most leisure, and the most inclination, to meditate on it. Second, contempt of unnecessary riches and preferments. Third, the ability in judgement to divest himself of all fear, anger, hatred, love, and compassion. Fourth, and lastly, patience to hear; diligent attention in hearing; and memory to retain, digest, and apply what he has heard.

The difference and division of the laws has been made in various ways, according to the different methods of those who have written of them. For it is something that depends not on nature, but on the writer's scope, and is subordinate to every man's chosen method. In the Institutes of Justinian, we find seven sorts of civil laws.
